lessons.title: Lesson 1: What CNC machines do and how they move
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the main CNC machines and point to their X, Y and Z axes.
This lesson builds toward: Given pictures or descriptions of shop machines and parts, you will name the CNC machine that makes each part and point to its X, Y and Z axes, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
CNC stands for computer numerical control. A CNC machine follows a program to move a cutting tool or a part along exact paths. Machining means cutting material away, in chips, until the part is the right shape and size.
A CNC mill (or machining center) holds the part still on a table while a spinning tool cuts it. It makes flat faces, pockets, slots and holes, like a bracket or an engine plate. A CNC lathe (or turning center) spins the part while a still tool cuts it. It makes round parts, like shafts, pins and bushings. Shops also use CNC routers for wood and plastic, and CNC plasma and laser cutters for sheet metal.
Each direction a machine can move is an axis. On a typical vertical mill, X moves left and right, Y moves toward you and away from you, and Z moves up and down with the spindle. On a lathe, Z runs along the length of the spinning part and X runs across it, which sets the diameter. Bigger machines add rotary axes, so a "5-axis" machine can tilt and turn the part too.
Words to know:
- CNC: computer numerical control: a machine that follows a program of numbers and codes.
- Mill: a machine where a spinning tool cuts a part held on a table.
- Lathe: a machine where the part spins and a still tool cuts it; makes round parts.
- Spindle: the part of the machine that spins the tool (mill) or the part (lathe).
- Axis: one direction a machine can move, such as X, Y or Z.
Try it now: Find three metal or plastic parts at home (a bolt, a door hinge, a pen cap, a bike part). For each, write "mill" or "lathe" and why. Then sketch a vertical mill as a box with a spindle on top and mark X, Y and Z with arrows.
You can now say what a CNC mill and a CNC lathe make and point to the X, Y and Z axes on each.

check.q: A shop needs 500 round steel pins. Which machine fits best?
check.why: A lathe spins the part, so it makes round parts like pins and shafts.

check.q: On a typical vertical mill, which axis moves the spindle up and down?
check.why: On a vertical mill, Z is the up-and-down axis of the spindle.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Reading a print: dimensions and tolerances
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write the smallest and largest allowed size for a toleranced dimension and decide if a part passes.
This lesson builds toward: Given a simple part print with toleranced dimensions, you will write the smallest and largest allowed size for each dimension and decide if a measured part passes, with no math errors on 3 dimensions.
A print (also called a blueprint or drawing) shows the part from different sides and gives every size you need. Each size is a dimension. US shops often use inches written to three or four decimal places; many shops use millimeters. The title block, in a corner of the print, shows the part name, the material, the units and the general tolerance.
No part can be made perfectly, so the print says how far off a size may be. That allowance is the tolerance. "1.000 ±0.005" means the size may be from 0.995 to 1.005 inches. These two numbers are the limits. If a dimension has no tolerance written next to it, the general tolerance in the title block applies.
Machinists check sizes with measuring tools. Calipers measure outside, inside and depth sizes quickly. A micrometer measures more precisely over a small range. Tools are kept clean and checked against a known standard, because a dirty or dropped tool can give a wrong reading.
Step by step:
- Find the dimension and its units (inch or mm) on the print.
- Find its tolerance next to it, or the general tolerance in the title block.
- Subtract the tolerance for the smallest size; add it for the largest size.
- Compare the measured size: if it is between the limits, the dimension passes.
Words to know:
- Print: a drawing of a part with all its sizes; also called a blueprint.
- Dimension: a size shown on a print, such as a length, width or hole diameter.
- Tolerance: how far a size may be off and still be good, such as ±0.005.
- Limits: the smallest and largest allowed size.
- Title block: the box on a print with the part name, material, units and general tolerance.
- Caliper / micrometer: measuring tools; the micrometer is more precise over a small range.
Try it now: Practice only. Work out the limits for: (a) 2.500 ±0.010, (b) 0.750 ±0.002, (c) 25.0 ±0.1 mm. Then decide: a part measured at 0.753 for (b), does it pass? (Answers: a 2.490 to 2.510; b 0.748 to 0.752; c 24.9 to 25.1 mm; 0.753 is too big, so it fails.)
You can now find a dimension and its tolerance on a print, work out its limits, and decide if a measured part passes.

check.q: A print says 1.250 ±0.003. What are the limits?
check.why: Subtract 0.003 for the smallest size and add 0.003 for the largest.

check.q: A dimension has no tolerance written next to it. Where do you look?
options: The general tolerance in the title block
check.why: The title block gives the general tolerance for dimensions without their own.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Reading a short CNC program
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Explain what each line of a short G-code program does and sketch its toolpath.
This lesson builds toward: Given a short CNC program of 8 to 12 lines, you will explain what each G-code and M-code line does and sketch the toolpath on graph paper, with the moves and the start and end points correct.
Most CNC machines read a program written in G-code. Each line, called a block, gives one or a few instructions. G-codes mostly tell the machine how to move. M-codes turn machine functions on and off. Letters with numbers give the details: X, Y and Z are positions, F is the feed rate (how fast the tool moves while cutting), S is the spindle speed, and T picks a tool.
Common codes on many machines: G00 is a rapid move (fast, not cutting). G01 is a straight cutting move at the feed rate. G02 and G03 cut arcs, clockwise and counterclockwise. G20 sets inches and G21 sets millimeters. G90 means positions are measured from the part's zero point (absolute). M03 starts the spindle clockwise, M05 stops it, M08 turns coolant on, M09 turns it off, and M30 ends the program.
Codes can differ from one machine control to another, so a machinist always checks the manual for the machine in front of them. Many shops write programs with CAM software, but machinists still read the code to catch mistakes before the tool moves. A free browser G-code viewer can draw a program's path, but graph paper works just as well for practice.
Step by step:
- Read the first lines: units (G20 or G21) and absolute mode (G90).
- Find the tool (T), spindle speed (S) and spindle start (M03).
- For each move, note the code (G00 or G01) and the X, Y and Z position.
- Plot each X and Y point on graph paper and join them in order: dashed for rapid, solid for cutting.
- Find the end: spindle stop (M05), coolant off (M09) and program end (M30).
Words to know:
- G-code: the codes, mostly for moves, that a CNC machine reads.
- M-code: codes that turn machine functions on or off, like the spindle or coolant.
- Block: one line of a CNC program.
- Feed rate (F): how fast the tool moves while it cuts.
- Spindle speed (S): how fast the spindle turns, in revolutions per minute.
- Toolpath: the path the tool follows.
- CAM: software that turns a 3D model into a CNC program.
Try it now: Practice only, on graph paper (1 square = 0.1 inch). Explain each line, then plot it: G20 G90 / T1 M06 / S1500 M03 / G00 X0 Y0 / G00 Z0.1 / G01 Z-0.05 F5.0 / G01 X1.0 / G01 Y1.0 / G01 X0 / G01 Y0 / G00 Z1.0 / M05 / M30. You should get a 1-inch square cut 0.05 inch deep.
You can now read a short CNC program line by line and sketch the path the tool will follow.

check.q: What does G01 X2.0 F10.0 tell the machine to do?
options: Rapid move to X2.0 without cutting
Cut in a straight line to X2.0 at feed rate 10
check.why: G01 is a straight cutting move, and F sets the feed rate.

check.q: Which code usually starts the spindle turning clockwise?
check.why: M03 is spindle on clockwise on most controls; M30 ends the program and M09 is coolant off.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Setup, safety and your path

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Setting up and making a first part
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Put the steps of a safe setup and first part in the right order.
This lesson builds toward: Given the steps of a setup and first part in mixed order, you will put the steps of a safe setup and first part in the right order, with the dry run and first-article inspection before production.
Before a shop makes many parts, someone sets up the machine and proves the program. New operators often start by loading parts and checking sizes, then learn setup under a lead machinist.
Setup means: read the print and the setup sheet, clean the table or chuck, hold the part firmly (workholding, such as a vise or chuck), load the right tools, and set the offsets. The work offset tells the machine where the part's zero point is. The tool offset tells it how long each tool is, so the tip lands in the right place.
Then the program is proven slowly. A dry run moves the machine with the tool safely above the part. Single block runs one line at a time. The feed override knob slows the moves, and the operator keeps a hand near the feed hold or emergency stop. After the first part is cut, it is measured against every dimension on the print. This is the first-article inspection. Only when it passes do production parts begin.
Step by step:
- Read the print, setup sheet and program.
- Clean the table, vise or chuck and hold the part firmly.
- Load the tools listed on the setup sheet.
- Set the work offset and tool offsets.
- Dry run above the part, then run single block with the feed override turned down.
- Measure the first part against every dimension (first-article inspection).
- Start production only after the first part passes; keep checking parts as you go.
Words to know:
- Setup sheet: the paper that lists the tools, workholding and offsets for a job.
- Workholding: what holds the part still, such as a vise, clamps or a chuck.
- Work offset: the setting that tells the machine where the part's zero point is.
- Tool offset: the setting for each tool's length (and size), so the tip lands in the right place.
- Dry run: running the program with the tool safely clear of the part.
- First-article inspection: measuring the first part against the whole print before making more.
Try it now: Write each of these on a slip of paper, mix them up, then put them in order: set tool offsets; first-article inspection; clean and hold the part; dry run; read the print and setup sheet; single block run; set the work offset; load tools; start production. Check your order against the steps in this lesson.
You can now put the steps of a setup and first part in order and say why the dry run and first-article inspection come before production.

check.q: Which setting tells the machine where the part's zero point is?
check.why: The work offset locates the part's zero; tool offsets set each tool's length.

check.q: The first part is cut. What comes before running the rest of the job?
options: Measure it against every dimension on the print
Turn the feed override to the maximum
Remove the guards to see better
check.why: First-article inspection proves the setup and program before production.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Staying safe in the machine shop
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name a control for each common machine shop hazard.
This lesson builds toward: Given five common machine shop hazards, you will name a control for each hazard: guard, protective gear, safe habit or lockout, naming a correct control for all five.
Machines can cause crushed fingers or hands, amputations, burns and blindness. The main hazards are the spinning spindle, chuck and tool, flying chips, sharp hot chips and edges, coolant on the skin, heavy parts and noise. OSHA's machine guarding rules (29 CFR 1910.212) require guards that protect workers from these hazards.
Shop habits: wear safety glasses with side shields at all times, and hearing protection where it is loud. Keep the machine doors and guards closed while it runs, and never reach in until the spindle has fully stopped. Most shops do not allow gloves, loose sleeves, jewelry or loose long hair near a turning spindle, because they can be caught and pull you in. Remove chips with a chip hook or brush, never your hands, and never blow chips at yourself or others. Wash coolant off your skin and read the safety data sheet (SDS).
When a machine is cleaned, repaired or serviced, its power is shut off and locked so no one can start it. This is lockout/tagout, covered by OSHA's rule on hazardous energy (29 CFR 1910.147), and only trained, authorized workers do it. Hands-on safety is taught in the shop by a qualified instructor; follow your shop's rules every time.
Step by step:
- Put on safety glasses with side shields, and hearing protection where needed.
- Remove gloves, jewelry and loose sleeves; tie back long hair.
- Check that guards and doors are in place and closed.
- Wait for the spindle to stop fully before opening the door or reaching in.
- Clear chips with a chip hook or brush, not your hands.
- For cleaning or repairs, follow the shop's lockout/tagout steps.
Words to know:
- Guard: a cover or door that keeps hands and chips away from moving parts.
- Chips: the small curls and bits of metal or plastic the tool cuts off; often sharp and hot.
- Coolant: the liquid that cools the tool and part and washes chips away.
- SDS: safety data sheet: the paper that lists a product's dangers and protection.
- Lockout/tagout: shutting off and locking a machine's power so no one can start it during service.
Official sources:
- OSHA: Machine Guarding standards
- OSHA: Control of Hazardous Energy (Lockout/Tagout)
Try it now: Make a two-column table on paper: Hazard and Control. Fill in five rows: spinning spindle, flying chips, sharp hot chips, coolant on skin, machine being repaired. Write one control for each, then check them against this lesson.
You can now name the main machine shop hazards and a control for each one.

check.q: A pile of hot chips is building up near the vise. How do you clear it?
options: Brush them off with your hand
Blow them off with air toward a coworker
Reach in while the spindle turns
Wait for a full stop, then use a chip hook or brush
check.why: Chips are sharp and hot; a chip hook or brush keeps your hands safe.

check.q: A machine needs a repair inside. What must happen first?
options: Its power is shut off and locked out by an authorized worker
Open the door while it runs
check.why: Lockout/tagout keeps anyone from starting the machine during service.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Training, credentials and your CNC plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a dated plan to get trained and earn a machining credential.
This lesson builds toward: Using official training, apprenticeship and NIMS pages, you will write a dated plan to get trained and earn a machining credential, with two programs, one credential and a date for each step.
Most machinists learn on the job, often starting as machine operators. Community colleges and technical schools offer certificates and two-year degrees that cover blueprint reading and CNC programming and operation. Registered apprenticeships combine paid work with classes and usually last several years. Search for one with the Apprenticeship Job Finder on apprenticeship.gov. Veterans can ask about using their education benefits, and young people can ask about programs at their school or job center.
Credentials show an employer what you can do. The National Institute for Metalworking Skills (NIMS) sets standards and credentials for machining job roles. Most NIMS credentials have two parts: an exam on the knowledge for the role, and a hands-on performance check, such as machining a part to the print. Check the current credential names and requirements on nims-skills.org. Some employers also value CNC or CAD/CAM certificates from a school or a machine maker.
This course prepares you; it does not certify you. Be careful with any program that promises a job or a credential fast for a big fee. Ask the school about shop time on real machines, which credentials it prepares you for, and how many graduates get hired.
Step by step:
- Choose a first goal: operator job, school program or apprenticeship.
- Find two programs near you: a community college or technical school, and an apprenticeship on apprenticeship.gov.
- Look up the NIMS credential for the job role you want on nims-skills.org.
- Ask each program about machine time, credentials, cost and job placement.
- Write a date for each step: apply, start, practice, test.
Words to know:
- Apprenticeship: a paid job with on-the-job training and classes, often for several years.
- Credential: proof, such as a certificate, that you passed a test of your skills.
- NIMS: the National Institute for Metalworking Skills, which sets machining standards and credentials.
- Performance check: a hands-on test where you do the task, such as machining a part to the print.
Official sources:
- NIMS: Credentialing
- Apprenticeship.gov (US Department of Labor)
- BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook: Machinists and Tool and Die Makers
Try it now: Final task: make your CNC starter plan. Sketch a mill and a lathe with their axes, work out the limits for three toleranced sizes, write and explain a short program for a square or slot and plot it, write your setup and safety checklist, and write a dated plan with two programs near you and one NIMS credential from the official site.
You can now find machining training near you, name the credential you will aim for, and follow a dated plan to get there.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Machines and axes The sketch mixes up the mill and the lathe, or the axes are missing or wrong. The mill and lathe are sketched with X, Y and Z marked correctly. Also names a part each machine makes and where a 5-axis machine adds motion. Print reading One or more limits are wrong, or the pass/fail call is wrong. All three dimensions have the right limits and a correct pass/fail call. Also shows a millimeter example and says which tool they would measure each size with. Program and toolpath Lines are not explained, or the plotted path does not match the code. Each line is explained and the sketched path matches the code, rapids and cuts marked. Also spots and fixes one mistake planted in the program by a partner or instructor. Setup and safety checklist The checklist leaves out guards, eye protection, clothing or chips. Covers guards, eye and hearing protection, clothing, chips, coolant and lockout for service. Also explains why each item matters in one short line. Setup order Production starts before the dry run or first-article inspection. Steps are in order, with offsets, a dry run and first-article inspection before production. Also adds in-process checks during the run. Dated plan No real programs, no credential, or no dates. Two real programs near the learner, one NIMS credential from the official site and a date for each step. Also lists questions asked of each program and the answers. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Where can you search for registered apprenticeships in the US?
options: A job ad that asks for a fee to apply
The Apprenticeship Job Finder on apprenticeship.gov
check.why: Apprenticeship.gov is the official US Department of Labor site with a job finder.

check.q: What do most NIMS credentials include?
options: An exam and a hands-on performance check
check.why: NIMS describes an exam on the role's knowledge plus a performance evaluation.
